title: "Module 4 — Measures of central tendency"
subtitle: "Data Description | Part II — Summarising one variable"
date-modified: 2026-10-18
---

**The business question.** "The Wandering Fork" has 120 days of daily
revenue data per franchise. The owner wants "one typical number" to put
in a report — but which one? The mean, the median, and the mode can
give different answers, especially when the data is skewed. This module
teaches you to compute all three, understand when they diverge, and
choose the right one for the business question. We start with five days
of one truck, small enough to compute by hand, and only then write the
formulas.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Compute the arithmetic mean, median, and mode of raw data.
- Compute the grouped-data mean (using class midpoints) and the
  weighted mean (for portfolio returns, GPA, etc.).
- Explain why the mean, median, and mode can differ, and choose the
  most appropriate one for a given business question.
- Read $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i$ aloud as a sentence, and
  write a sum described in words with the $\sum$ symbol and the
  subscript $x_i$.
- Prove that the arithmetic mean is the value that minimizes the sum
  of squared deviations — the property that makes it the natural
  partner of the variance (Module 6).

## Theory

### One typical day?

A Wandering Fork truck ("Festival") recorded its revenue over five
days, one of which was a big local event. The numbers are a simplified
extract chosen so that you can compute everything by hand.

| Day | Truck C "Festival" (€) |
|---|---:|
| 1 | 580 |
| 2 | 590 |
| 3 | 600 |
| 4 | 610 |
| 5 | 1,320 |

The owner wants to tell the bank what an everyday day looks like. Four
days brought in about €600 and one brought in more than twice that.
What single number would you put in the report — and would you be
comfortable defending it?

### Arithmetic mean

**Try it.** Truck C's revenue over $n = 5$ days is below. Add up the
five values, then split the total evenly across the days.

| Day $i$ | $x_i$ (€) |
|---|---:|
| 1 | 580 |
| 2 | 590 |
| 3 | 600 |
| 4 | 610 |
| 5 | 1,320 |
| **Total** | **?** |
| **Total ÷ 5** | **?** |

How many of the five days earned less than your result?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

- Total: $580+590+600+610+1{,}320 = 3{,}700$.
- Split evenly: $3{,}700 / 5 = 740$ €.
- Four of the five days earned less than €740: the one festival day
  pulled the mean up.

</details>

**See it.** The figure draws the five days as dots on a revenue axis.
Step 2 draws the distance from each dot to the mean: the days below
(red) exactly offset the day above (green), so the mean is the balance
point of the dots.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
truckC = [580, 590, 600, 610, 1320]
sortedC = [...truckC].sort((a, b) => a - b)
nC = truckC.length
meanC = truckC.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / nC
medianC = (sortedC[Math.floor((nC - 1) / 2)]
  + sortedC[Math.ceil((nC - 1) / 2)]) / 2
fmtC = v => Math.round(v).toLocaleString("en-US")
signedC = v => (v > 0 ? "+" : v < 0 ? "−" : "") + fmtC(Math.abs(v))

viewof step = {
  const labels = ["1 · Dots", "2 · Mean", "3 · Median"];
  const form = html`<form class="ojs-step-picker">Show: ${labels.map((l, i) =>
    html`<label> <input type="radio" name="step" value="${i + 1}"
      ${i === 0 ? "checked" : ""}> ${l} </label>`)}</form>`;
  form.value = 1;
  form.oninput = () => {
    form.value = +form.querySelector("input:checked").value;
  };
  return form;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 660, H = 210, rowH = 24, top = 40;
  const BLUE = "steelblue", ORANGE = "darkorange", PURPLE = "mediumpurple";
  const POS = "#5cb85c", NEG = "#d9534f";
  const x = v => 70 + (v - 500) * (W - 100) / (1400 - 500);
  let g = "";

  truckC.forEach((v, i) => {
    const y = top + i * rowH;
    g += `<text x="8" y="${y + 4}" fill="currentColor"
      font-size="12">Day ${i + 1}</text>`;
    if (step === 2) {
      const d = v - meanC;
      const c = d > 0 ? POS : NEG;
      g += `<line x1="${x(meanC)}" x2="${x(v)}" y1="${y}" y2="${y}"
        stroke="${c}" stroke-width="3"/>`;
      g += `<text x="${x(v) + (d > 0 ? 10 : -10)}" y="${y + 4}"
        text-anchor="${d > 0 ? "start" : "end"}" fill="${c}"
        font-size="12">${signedC(d)}</text>`;
    }
    g += `<circle cx="${x(v)}" cy="${y}" r="6" fill="${BLUE}"/>`;
  });

  if (step === 2) {
    g += `<line x1="${x(meanC)}" x2="${x(meanC)}" y1="${top - 18}"
      y2="${top + nC * rowH - 8}" stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2"
      stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(meanC) + 6}" y="${top - 24}" fill="${ORANGE}"
      font-size="12">mean = ${fmtC(meanC)}</text>`;
  }
  if (step === 3) {
    g += `<line x1="${x(medianC)}" x2="${x(medianC)}" y1="${top - 18}"
      y2="${top + nC * rowH - 8}" stroke="${PURPLE}" stroke-width="2"
      stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(medianC) - 6}" y="${top - 24}" text-anchor="end"
      fill="${PURPLE}" font-size="12">median = ${fmtC(medianC)}</text>`;
    g += `<line x1="${x(meanC)}" x2="${x(meanC)}" y1="${top - 18}"
      y2="${top + nC * rowH - 8}" stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2"
      stroke-dasharray="2 4"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(meanC) + 6}" y="${top - 24}" fill="${ORANGE}"
      font-size="12">mean = ${fmtC(meanC)}</text>`;
  }

  for (let t = 600; t <= 1400; t += 200) {
    g += `<line x1="${x(t)}" x2="${x(t)}" y1="${H - 30}" y2="${H - 24}"
      stroke="currentColor"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(t)}" y="${H - 10}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="12">€${fmtC(t)}</text>`;
  }
  g += `<line x1="${x(500)}" x2="${x(1400)}" y1="${H - 30}" y2="${H - 30}"
    stroke="currentColor"/>`;
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
    aria-label="Truck C daily revenue as dots with its mean and median">
    ${g}</svg>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const devs = truckC.map(v => v - meanC);
  const sumDev = devs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const k = (nC + 1) / 2;
  const below = sortedC.filter(v => v < medianC).length;
  const above = sortedC.filter(v => v > medianC).length;
  const line = step === 1
    ? `Truck C: ${nC} days, from €${fmtC(sortedC[0])} to €${fmtC(sortedC[nC - 1])}.`
    : step === 2
    ? `Distances to the mean (€${fmtC(meanC)}): ${devs.map(signedC).join(", ")} — sum = ${fmtC(sumDev)}.`
    : `Ordered values: ${sortedC.map(fmtC).join(", ")}. Position ${k} holds €${fmtC(medianC)}: ${below} days below, ${above} above. The mean (€${fmtC(meanC)}) is dragged far to the right of the median.`;
  return html`<p><em>${line}</em></p>`;
}
```

In plain words: the mean is the "fair share" — what each day would earn
if the total were split evenly across the days.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — arithmetic mean
The **arithmetic mean** (or average) $\bar{x}$ of $n$ values
$x_1,\dots,x_n$ is their sum divided by their count. It uses every
single observation, which makes it efficient but also sensitive to
extreme values: one very large or very small $x_i$ pulls $\bar{x}$
toward it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — arithmetic mean
$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i.
$$
In plain terms: add up all the observations, then split the total
evenly across them — the "if everyone got the same amount" value.
:::

#### Notation decoder: arithmetic mean

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (Truck C) |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | "n" | 5 days |
| $x_i$ | "x sub i" | the value on day $i$, e.g. $x_3 = 600$ |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{n}$ | "add up, for i from 1 to n" | $x_1+x_2+\dots+x_5 = 3{,}700$ |
| $\frac{1}{n}$ | "one over n", i.e. "divided by n" | ÷ 5 |
| $\bar{x}$ | "x-bar" | the mean, 740 € |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the mean is one over $n$ times the sum,
for $i$ from 1 to $n$, of the values $x_i$ — in other words, add up all
$n$ values and divide by $n$."

The small number $i$ under $x$ is only a label: $x_1$ is the first
day's value, $x_2$ the second's, and so on up to $x_n$. The symbol
$\sum_{i=1}^{n}$ is a loop written compactly: start with $i=1$, add
$x_i$, move to $i=2$, and continue until $i=n$.

### Median

**Try it.** Put Truck C's five values in order, from smallest to
largest, and find the one in the middle.

| Rank | Ordered value (€) |
|---|---:|
| 1st | ? |
| 2nd | ? |
| 3rd | ? |
| 4th | ? |
| 5th | ? |

1. Which rank holds the middle value? How many days are below it and how
   many above?
2. Compare it with the mean you found above (740).

Your turn: the first four days of Truck A "Steady" were 590, 610, 630
and 630. There is no single middle day any more: what would you report?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

- Ordered: 580, 590, 600, 610, 1,320 (already in order here).
- The middle rank is the 3rd: the median is **600** €, with 2 days below
  and 2 days above. The mean (740) is far above it; the median ignores
  how big the festival day was.
- Truck A, four days: the middle sits between the 2nd and 3rd values, so
  take their average: $(610+630)/2 = 620$ €.

</details>

**See it.** Step 3 of the figure above adds the median line: it sits
where the ordered list reaches its middle, while the mean (dotted) is
dragged toward the festival day.

In plain words: the median is the middle of the ordered list — half the
days earn less, half earn more — so only the ranking matters, not how
extreme the largest day is.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — median
The **median** $Me$ is the value that splits an ordered series into
two equal halves: at least 50% of observations are $\leq Me$ and at
least 50% are $\geq Me$. Unlike the mean, the median only cares about
the *rank* of each value, not its magnitude, so a single extreme
observation cannot drag it far.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — median position
For $n$ ordered values, the median sits at position $(n+1)/2$: if
$n$ is odd this is a single observation; if $n$ is even, it is the
average of the two middle observations. This is exactly the quantile
formula with $p=0.5$ (see Module 5).
:::

#### Notation decoder: median position

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (Truck C, then Truck A) |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | "n" | 5 days (Truck C); 4 days (Truck A's first four) |
| $(n+1)/2$ | "n plus one, over two" | position 3 for $n=5$; position 2.5 for $n=4$ |
| $Me$ | "M-e", the median | 600 € (Truck C); 620 € (Truck A) |
| $p=0.5$ | "p equals one half" | the half-way point: half the days below, half above |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "after sorting the $n$ values, the
median is the value at position $n+1$ over two; if that position falls
between two days, average those two days."

### Mode

**Try it.** Truck A "Steady" earned 590, 610, 630, 630 and 640 € over
five days. Count how often each value appears.

| Value (€) | Number of days |
|---|---:|
| 590 | ? |
| 610 | ? |
| 630 | ? |
| 640 | ? |

Which value is the most frequent? Does Truck C (all five values
different) have one?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Value (€) | Number of days |
|---|---:|
| 590 | 1 |
| 610 | 1 |
| 630 | 2 |
| 640 | 1 |

- The most frequent value is **630** €: Truck A's mode.
- Truck C has no repeated value, hence no mode on raw data: with
  continuous revenue figures this is the usual situation, which is why
  the next section groups the data into classes.

</details>

**See it.** On a bar chart of the counts above, the mode is the tallest
bar:

```
 590 | █
 610 | █
 630 | ██   <- mode
 640 | █
```

In plain words: the mode is the most popular value — the tallest bar,
the most crowded spot on the number line.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — mode
The **mode** $Mo$ is the most frequently occurring value (for
discrete or categorical data) or the center of the most frequent
*class* (for grouped continuous data — the "peak" of the histogram
from Module 3). A distribution can have one mode (unimodal), two
(bimodal), or more.
:::

### Mode of grouped data

**Try it.** Ten days of a street-food truck are grouped into classes of
width $h = 100$ €:

| Class (€) | Frequency |
|---|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 1 |
| [500, 600[ | 4 |
| [600, 700[ | 3 |
| [700, 800[ | 2 |

1. Which class is the modal class? What is its lower bound $L$?
2. Which frequencies come just before and just after it?
3. Compute the gap $f_1 - f_0$ and the gap $f_1 - f_2$. Which neighbour
   is closer in frequency?
4. The mode sits a fraction
   $\frac{f_1-f_0}{(f_1-f_0)+(f_1-f_2)}$ of the way across the class.
   Compute it and place the mode.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

1. The modal class is $[500, 600[$ (highest frequency, 4); $L=500$.
2. Before: $f_0 = 1$; after: $f_2 = 3$.
3. $f_1-f_0 = 3$ and $f_1-f_2 = 1$: the next class (frequency 3)
   competes harder.
4. Fraction $= 3/(3+1) = 0.75$, so $Mo = 500 + 100 \times 0.75 = 575$ €.
   The mode is pulled toward the right edge of the class, where the
   competing neighbour is.

</details>

**See it.** The same table as a histogram, one block per day, placed at
the class midpoints:

```
 450 | █
 550 | ████   <- modal class [500, 600[
 650 | ███
 750 | ██
```

The modal class has a tall right neighbour (3) and a short left
neighbour (1), so the peak leans right of the class midpoint (550): 575.

In plain words: inside the modal class, lean toward the neighbour that
competes harder; the mode estimates the top of the histogram's hill.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — mode of grouped continuous data
For continuous data grouped into classes of equal width $h$, the
mode is estimated by linear interpolation *inside* the modal class
(the class with the highest frequency $f_1$):
$$
Mo = L + h \cdot \frac{f_1-f_0}{(f_1-f_0)+(f_1-f_2)},
$$
where $L$ is the modal class's lower bound, $f_0$ is the frequency
of the preceding class, and $f_2$ is the frequency of the following
class. Intuitively, the mode leans toward whichever neighboring
class is "competing" harder with the modal class for observations:
a much lower $f_0$ than $f_2$ pulls the estimated mode toward the
left edge of the class, and vice versa.
:::

#### Notation decoder: mode of grouped continuous data

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (ten-day table) |
|---|---|---|
| $Mo$ | "M-o", the mode | 575 € |
| $L$ | "L" | lower bound of the modal class, 500 |
| $h$ | "h" | class width, 100 |
| $f_1$ | "f sub 1" | frequency of the modal class, 4 |
| $f_0$ | "f sub 0" | frequency of the class before, 1 |
| $f_2$ | "f sub 2" | frequency of the class after, 3 |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the mode is the modal class's lower
bound plus the class width times a fraction: the lead over the class
before, divided by the lead over the class before plus the lead over the
class after."

### Grouped-data mean

**Try it.** Same ten-day table. Pretend every day sits exactly at the
midpoint of its class, then compute the usual mean.

| Class (€) | Midpoint $m_i$ | Frequency $f_i$ | $f_i \times m_i$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 450 | 1 | ? |
| [500, 600[ | ? | 4 | ? |
| [600, 700[ | ? | 3 | ? |
| [700, 800[ | ? | 2 | ? |
| **Total** | | **?** | **?** |

Divide the last total by the total frequency.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Class (€) | Midpoint $m_i$ | Frequency $f_i$ | $f_i \times m_i$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 450 | 1 | 450 |
| [500, 600[ | 550 | 4 | 2,200 |
| [600, 700[ | 650 | 3 | 1,950 |
| [700, 800[ | 750 | 2 | 1,500 |
| **Total** | | **10** | **6,100** |

$6{,}100 / 10 = 610$ € — an approximation, since we do not know where
inside each class the days really fell.

</details>

**See it.** In the histogram above, the 10 blocks sit at 450, 550, 550,
550, 550, 650, 650, 650, 750, 750. Their balance point is 610, to the
right of the mode (575): the mean uses every block, the mode only the
tallest column.

In plain words: treat every observation in a class as if it were
exactly at the class midpoint, then compute the usual mean. The
approximation error is exactly the information lost when data is
grouped.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — grouped-data mean
When raw data is unavailable and only a class frequency table exists,
the mean is approximated using class midpoints $m_i$:
$$
\bar{x}_{\text{grouped}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i m_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i}
= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i m_i}{n},
$$
where $n_i$ is the count in class $i$, $m_i = (L_i + L_i + h)/2$ is
the class midpoint, and $k$ is the number of classes. This is a
weighted mean where the weights are the class frequencies.
:::

#### Notation decoder: grouped-data mean

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (ten-day table) |
|---|---|---|
| $\bar{x}_{\text{grouped}}$ | "x-bar, grouped" | 610 € |
| $k$ | "k" | 4 classes |
| $i$ | "i" | the class number, from 1 to 4 |
| $m_i$ | "m sub i" | class midpoint, e.g. $m_2 = 550$ |
| $f_i$, $n_i$ | "f sub i", "n sub i" | class frequency, e.g. $n_2 = 4$ |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{k}$ | "add up, for i from 1 to k" | the Total row: 6,100 and 10 |
| $n$ | "n" | total count, 10 days |
| $L_i$ | "L sub i" | lower bound of class $i$, e.g. $L_2 = 500$ |
| $h$ | "h" | class width, 100 |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the grouped mean is the sum, over all
$k$ classes, of frequency times midpoint, divided by the total
frequency."

### Weighted mean

**Try it.** The Wandering Fork has three sites. The numbers are a
simplified extract: the mean daily revenue per truck, and the number of
trucks at each site.

| Site $i$ | Mean daily revenue $x_i$ (€) | Trucks $w_i$ | $w_i \times x_i$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Harbour | 600 | 3 | ? |
| Campus | 500 | 1 | ? |
| Station | 800 | 1 | ? |
| **Total** | | **?** | **?** |

1. Compute the plain average of the three site means, ignoring trucks.
2. Compute the average revenue *per truck*: total of the last column
   divided by the total number of trucks. Why is it different?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Site $i$ | $x_i$ (€) | $w_i$ | $w_i \times x_i$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Harbour | 600 | 3 | 1,800 |
| Campus | 500 | 1 | 500 |
| Station | 800 | 1 | 800 |
| **Total** | | **5** | **3,100** |

1. $(600+500+800)/3 = 633.33$ € — it treats each site as equal.
2. $3{,}100 / 5 = 620$ € per truck. It is lower because Harbour, with a
   below-average mean, hosts three of the five trucks and so counts
   three times.

</details>

**See it.** Each truck is one "vote" for its site's mean:

```
 Harbour  600 | ● ● ●
 Campus   500 | ●
 Station  800 | ●
```

Five votes (600, 600, 600, 500, 800) average to 620; Station, with
one truck, cannot pull the result as far as Harbour can.

In plain words: multiply each value by its weight, sum the products,
and divide by the total weight. The ordinary mean is the special case
where all weights are equal.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — weighted mean
When observations carry different importance (weights $w_i$), the
**weighted mean** is
$$
\bar{x}_w = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i}.
$$
Common business uses: portfolio return (weights = amounts invested),
GPA (weights = credit hours), price indices (weights = quantities).
:::

#### Notation decoder: weighted mean

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (three sites) |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | "n" | 3 sites |
| $x_i$ | "x sub i" | site $i$'s mean revenue, e.g. $x_1 = 600$ |
| $w_i$ | "w sub i" | site $i$'s weight (trucks), e.g. $w_1 = 3$ |
| $w_i x_i$ | "w sub i times x sub i" | the last column: 1,800, 500, 800 |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{n}$ | "add up, for i from 1 to n" | numerator 3,100; denominator 5 |
| $\bar{x}_w$ | "x-bar, weighted" | 620 € |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the weighted mean is the sum, over all
$n$ values, of weight times value, divided by the sum of the weights."

### Choosing the right measure

Back to Truck C: its mean (740) and median (600) disagree because of one
festival day. Which one answers the owner's question depends on what the
question is.

::: {.callout-warning}
#### When to use which
- **Mean**: symmetric distributions, no outliers, when you need the
  value that feeds into variance/standard deviation (Modules 6–7).
- **Median**: skewed distributions, ordinal data, or when outliers
  would distort the mean.
- **Mode**: nominal data, or to identify the most common category
  (e.g., the most popular product).
- **Weighted mean**: when observations have different importance
  (portfolio, GPA, indices).
- **Grouped mean**: only when raw data is unavailable; always state
  it is an approximation.
:::

## Worked example

We use the **Harbour 30-day subset** (sheet `harbour_30d`) and the
**payroll-skew.csv** dataset to illustrate the concepts of this
module.

### Harbour 30-day revenue (symmetric case)

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---:|
| Mean $\bar{x}$ | 628.34 |
| Median $Me$ | 643.63 |
| Grouped mode $Mo$ | 666.67 |

Class frequency table (class width 100, from Module 3):

| Class (€) | Frequency |
|---|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 6 |
| [500, 600[ | 6 |
| [600, 700[ | 8 |
| [700, 800[ | 7 |
| [800, 900[ | 3 |

**Step 1 — mean.** Summing all 30 daily revenues and dividing by 30
gives $\bar{x} = 628.34$: on average, "The Wandering Fork" brings in
about €628 per day.

**Step 2 — median.** As found in Module 5, $Me = 643.63$: half the
trading days earned less than this, half earned more.

**Step 3 — mode.** The modal class is $[600,700[$ with $f_1=8$,
flanked by $[500,600[$ ($f_0=6$) and $[700,800[$ ($f_2=7$). With
$L=600$ and $h=100$:
$$
Mo = 600 + 100 \times \frac{8-6}{(8-6)+(8-7)}
= 600 + 100 \times \frac{2}{3}
\approx 666.67.
$$
The single most "typical" revenue band, estimated from the histogram
shape, centers around €666.67.

**Putting it together.** The three indicators — 628.34, 643.63, and
666.67 — are all close to one another, which is itself informative:
it signals a roughly symmetric, well-behaved distribution rather
than one dominated by a skewed tail.

### Payroll skew (right-skewed case)

The `payroll-skew.csv` dataset contains 11 salaries: one CEO at
€180,000 and ten staff members between €25,000–€45,000.

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---:|
| Mean $\bar{x}$ | 47,231 |
| Median $Me$ | 38,050 |
| Mode $Mo$ | 25,166 (no unique mode; smallest value shown) |

**Step 1 — mean.** The CEO's €180,000 pulls the mean up to €47,231,
well above what 10 out of 11 employees earn.

**Step 2 — median.** The median (€38,050) is unaffected by the
extreme value and better represents a "typical" salary.

**Step 3 — mode.** No value repeats exactly; the distribution is
strongly right-skewed (skewness = 3.12), so the mean > median > mode
pattern holds.

## Proof / derivation

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Derivation — the mean minimizes the sum of squared deviations (click to expand)
Consider the function that measures the total squared "distance"
between every observation and some reference point $a$:
$$
f(a) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - a)^2.
$$
To find the value of $a$ that minimizes $f$, differentiate with
respect to $a$ and set the result to zero:
$$
f'(a) = -2\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - a) = 0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i - na = 0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
a = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = \bar{x}.
$$
The second derivative, $f''(a) = 2n > 0$, confirms this is a
minimum, not a maximum. In words: **no other single number sits
closer, on average in squared terms, to every observation than the
arithmetic mean does.** This is exactly why the variance (Module 6)
is defined as the average squared deviation *from the mean*
specifically — any other reference point would only make the total
squared deviation larger.
:::

## Visual intuition

Picture each day's revenue as a small weight placed on a number
line. The **mean** is the physical balance point (center of mass):
if the number line were a rigid rod, it would balance perfectly on a
pivot placed at $\bar{x}=628.34$. The **median** is a purely
positional idea: the point that has exactly as many weights to its
left as to its right, regardless of how heavy any of them are. The
**mode** is simply the tallest bar on the histogram — the single
most crowded spot on the number line. When the histogram is close to
symmetric, all three landmarks cluster near the same spot, which is
exactly the pattern seen above (628.34, 643.63, 666.67). When a
single extreme weight is added (the CEO's salary), the balance point
(mean) shifts dramatically, while the positional median barely moves.

## Exercises

All exercises below are done by hand; the Excel ones are in the
[homework](#homework-excel-lab).

::: {#exr-mean-vs-median name="Mean vs. median with an outlier"}
Five employee monthly salaries (in €k) are: 32, 35, 33, 34, 210.
Compute the mean and the median. Which one better represents a
"typical" salary here, and why?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Mean $= (32+35+33+34+210)/5 = 344/5 = 68.8$. Ordering
the values gives $32, 33, 34, 35, 210$, so the median (the middle
value) is $34$. The median is the better representative here: the
single very high salary (210) pulls the mean far above what four out
of five employees actually earn, while the median, using only rank,
is unaffected by how extreme that one value is.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-choosing-indicator name="Choosing an indicator for The Wandering Fork"}
The owner of "The Wandering Fork" asks for "one typical number" for
daily revenue. Given $\bar{x}=628.34$ and $Me=643.63$, which would
you recommend, and why?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Since Module 5 showed **zero outliers** in the daily
revenue data, the mean is not being distorted by extreme values, so
either indicator is defensible here. The mean is generally the
better recommendation in this specific case: it uses every one of
the 30 observations (not just their ranks), and it is the indicator
that feeds directly into the variance, standard deviation, and
coefficient of variation computed in Module 6 — keeping the
reporting consistent across the analysis.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-grouped-mode name="Grouped mode for a different class table"}
A rival street-food vendor's daily revenue has a modal class
$[500,600[$ ($L=500$, $h=100$) with frequency $f_1=18$, preceded by a
class with frequency $f_0=10$ and followed by a class with frequency
$f_2=15$. Estimate the grouped mode.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$$
Mo = 500 + 100 \times \frac{18-10}{(18-10)+(18-15)}
= 500 + 100 \times \frac{8}{11}
\approx 572.73.
$$
The estimated most-typical revenue band for the rival vendor centers
around €572.73 — lower than "The Wandering Fork"'s €666.67, and
leaning toward the lower-frequency neighboring class ($f_0=10$ vs.
$f_2=15$) rather than the middle of the modal class.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-formula-words name="Formula to words"}
(a) Read $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i$ aloud as one sentence.
Which indicator is it?

(b) Read $\bar{x}_w=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i}$
aloud as one sentence. Which indicator is it, and what does it become
when all $w_i$ are equal?

(c) For $x_1=4$, $x_2=6$, $x_3=8$, compute $\sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i$ and
$\bar{x}$.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

(a) "Add up the $n$ observations $x_1$ to $x_n$ and divide by $n$." It
is the arithmetic mean.

(b) "Multiply each value by its weight, add up the products, and divide
by the sum of the weights." It is the weighted mean; with equal weights
the $w_i$ cancel and it becomes the ordinary mean.

(c) $\sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i = 4+6+8 = 18$, so $\bar{x} = 18/3 = 6$.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-words-formula name="Words to formula"}
Write in symbols:

(a) "add up the first four observations";
(b) "the median position for $n$ ordered values";
(c) "the sum of weight times value over three sites";
(d) "the distance between the 2nd observation and the mean".

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

(a) $\sum_{i=1}^{4} x_i$.
(b) $(n+1)/2$.
(c) $\sum_{i=1}^{3} w_i x_i$.
(d) $x_2-\bar{x}$ (negative if the 2nd observation is below the mean).

</details>
:::

## Common mistakes

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Watch out
- **Using the mean for skewed data.** The payroll example shows how a
  single extreme value can make the mean misleading; the median is
  safer.
- **Forgetting to lock the total in a weighted mean.** The denominator
  `SUM(weights)` must be absolute or a structured reference,
  otherwise copying the formula shifts the total.
- **Confusing grouped mean with raw mean.** The grouped mean is an
  approximation; always state it as such and prefer the raw mean when
  available.
- **Using `MODE.SNGL` on continuous data.** Raw continuous data rarely
  has exact repeats; use the grouped mode formula instead.
- **Treating ordinal numbers as ratio.** `satisfaction_rating` is 1–5,
  but `=AVERAGE` on it is questionable; use the median.
:::

## Exit check

Five minutes, no calculator needed except for question 4.

1. In one sentence, what does the arithmetic mean measure?
2. Why can one extreme value move the mean a lot but the median hardly
   at all?
3. Read $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i$ aloud as a sentence.
4. Compute the mean, the median and the mode of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9.
5. A report must give "the typical salary" for a company with a few
   very high executive salaries. Which indicator do you choose, and why?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The "fair share": the value each observation would have if the total
   were split evenly (the balance point of the data).
2. The mean uses the size of every value, so a large one drags it; the
   median only uses the ranking, so the largest value could be 10 or
   10,000 without changing the middle position.
3. "Add up all $n$ observations, for $i$ from 1 to $n$, and divide the
   sum by $n$."
4. Mean $= 25/5 = 5$; median = the 3rd of the ordered values = 4; mode
   = 4 (appears twice).
5. The median: the executive salaries are outliers that would inflate
   the mean well above what most employees earn.

</details>

## Homework — Excel lab

Reproduce, in Excel, every indicator you computed by hand in class,
with `AVERAGE`, `MEDIAN`, `MODE.SNGL` and `SUMPRODUCT`, then apply them
to the full dataset.

**Estimated time:** about 50–60 minutes. Any spreadsheet application
works, at home or in a campus computer room.

**Follow-up:** a 10-minute debrief at the start of
[Module 5](module-05.qmd). Bring your Step 0 results and any question
on Homework 1–3.

### Using Excel

The complete list of function names, with their French equivalents, is
on the [Excel functions](excel-functions.qmd) page.

| Concept | Excel function / steps |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic mean | `=AVERAGE(range)` |
| Median | `=MEDIAN(range)` |
| Mode, raw data (single mode) | `=MODE.SNGL(range)` |
| Mode, raw data (all modes, array formula) | `=MODE.MULT(range)` |
| Weighted mean | `=SUMPRODUCT(values, weights)/SUM(weights)` |
| Grouped mean | No direct one-cell function — use `SUMPRODUCT(midpoints, frequencies)/SUM(frequencies)` |
| Mode, grouped continuous data | No direct one-cell function — use `FREQUENCY(range, bins)` to get $f_0, f_1, f_2$, then apply the interpolation formula manually |

For the **full table** (120 days per franchise) use the Excel Table
`tblFork` and add the franchise as one more condition, for example
`=AVERAGEIFS(tblFork[daily_revenue_eur], tblFork[franchise], "Harbour")`.

### Step 0 — check your class results

1. Type Truck C's five values (580, 590, 600, 610, 1320) in `A2:A6` and
   Truck A's (590, 610, 630, 630, 640) in `B2:B6`.
2. Below each column, compute `=AVERAGE(A2:A6)`, `=MEDIAN(A2:A6)` and
   `=MODE.SNGL(A2:A6)`. Repeat for column B.
3. Type the three site means (600, 500, 800) in `D2:D4` and the trucks
   (3, 1, 1) in `E2:E4`. Compute
   `=SUMPRODUCT(D2:D4,E2:E4)/SUM(E2:E4)` and compare it with
   `=AVERAGE(D2:D4)`.
4. Type the ten-day table's midpoints (450, 550, 650, 750) in `G2:G5`
   and its frequencies (1, 4, 3, 2) in `H2:H5`. Compute
   `=SUMPRODUCT(G2:G5,H2:H5)/SUM(H2:H5)`.
5. Compare every result with your hand computation.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Expected results</summary>

| Indicator | Truck C | Truck A |
|---|---:|---:|
| `AVERAGE` | 740 | 620 |
| `MEDIAN` | 600 | 630 |
| `MODE.SNGL` | `#N/A` (no repeat) | 630 |

| Indicator | Result |
|---|---:|
| Weighted mean of the sites (`SUMPRODUCT`) | 620 |
| Plain `AVERAGE` of the site means | 633.33 |
| Grouped mean of the ten-day table | 610 |

If `MODE.SNGL` shows `#N/A` for Truck C, that is expected: no value
appears twice. The grouped mode (575) has no one-cell function; apply
the interpolation formula by hand.

</details>

### Homework 1 (Excel) — Weighted mean for a portfolio

An investor holds three assets: €10,000 in Asset A (return 8%),
€20,000 in Asset B (return 5%), and €5,000 in Asset C (return 12%).
Compute the portfolio's weighted mean return.

**How to.** Use `SUMPRODUCT` on the amounts and the returns, divided by
`SUM` of the amounts.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

`=SUMPRODUCT({10000,20000,5000},{0.08,0.05,0.12})/SUM({10000,20000,5000})`
= 7.00%. The portfolio return is the weighted mean of the individual
returns, with weights equal to the amounts invested.

</details>

### Homework 2 (Excel) — Grouped mean from a class table

Using the Harbour 30-day class table from the worked example (five
classes of width 100, midpoints 450, 550, 650, 750, 850), compute the
grouped mean and compare it to the raw-data mean (628.34).

**How to.** Type the midpoints and the frequencies in two columns and
divide their `SUMPRODUCT` by `SUM` of the frequencies.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

`=SUMPRODUCT({450,550,650,750,850},{6,6,8,7,3})/SUM({6,6,8,7,3})`
= 19,000/30 = 633.33. The grouped mean (633.33) is close to the raw
mean (628.34) — the difference (about €5) is the approximation
error from using class midpoints instead of the exact 30 values.

</details>

### Homework 3 (Excel) — Campus revenue: mean, median, mode

In `wandering-fork.xlsx`, filter `franchise` to "Campus" and compute
the mean, median, and mode of `daily_revenue_eur` for all 120 days.
How do they compare to Harbour's values?

**How to.** Filter `franchise` to "Campus" (or use `AVERAGEIFS`), then
apply `AVERAGE`, `MEDIAN` and `MODE.SNGL`; repeat with "Harbour".

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Campus 120-day: mean = 455.03, median = 390.39, mode
(no unique mode). Over the same 120 days, Harbour has mean = 413.49
and median = 391.47. The medians are almost equal (390 vs 391), but
the Campus mean sits much further above its median (gap €65 vs €22),
confirming the stronger right skew seen in Module 7 (Campus
skewness = 1.00 vs Harbour's 0.47).

</details>
